A "serious incident" is an incident or malfunctioning of an AI system that directly or indirectly causes any of the following: the death of a person, or serious harm to a person’s health [1][49](1). It can also lead to a serious and irreversible disruption of the management or operation of critical infrastructure [1][49](1)(b). Furthermore, it may result in the infringement of obligations under Union law intended to protect fundamental rights [1][49](1)(c). A serious incident can also cause serious harm to property or the environment [1][49](1)(d).

A 'general-purpose AI model' is an AI model that displays significant generality and can competently perform a wide range of distinct tasks regardless of how it is placed on the market [1](1)(63). It can also be integrated into a variety of downstream systems or applications, unless the model is being used for research, development, or prototyping before it is placed on the market [1](1)(63). A 'general-purpose AI system' is an AI system that is based on a general-purpose AI model and has the capability to serve various purposes, both for direct use and for integration into other AI systems [4](4)(66).
This Regulation does not apply to obligations of deployers who are natural persons using AI systems in the course of a purely personal non-professional activity [1].

Research, testing, or development activities regarding AI systems or AI models prior to their being placed on the market or put into service are not covered by the exclusion in Article 2 [1]. However, the testing of high-risk AI systems must be performed, as appropriate, at any time throughout the development process, and in any event, prior to their being placed on the market or put into service [2]. Providers may conduct testing of high-risk AI systems in real world conditions at any time before the placing on the market or the putting into service of the high-risk AI system [3]. The AI Office is responsible for conformity assessments and tests of high-risk AI systems that are classified as high-risk and subject to a third-party conformity assessment before such AI systems are placed on the market or put into service [5].

Data governance and management practices for training, validation and testing data sets of a high-risk AI system must cover several aspects [1]. These practices must concern the relevant design choices [1](a). They must also cover data collection processes, the origin of the data, and the original purpose of personal data collection [1](b). Furthermore, the practices must address data-preparation processing operations such as annotation, labelling, cleaning, updating, enrichment, and aggregation [1](c). The governance must also include an assessment of the availability, quantity, and suitability of the data sets [1](e).

High-risk AI systems must technically allow for the automatic recording of events, which are referred to as logs, throughout the system's lifetime [3]. These logging capabilities must enable the recording of events relevant to identifying risks, facilitating post-market monitoring, and monitoring the system's operation [3]. Providers of high-risk AI systems are required to keep the logs automatically generated by their systems, to the extent those logs are under their control [1][4]. Deployers of high-risk AI systems must also keep the automatically generated logs under their control for a period of at least six months, unless different Union or national law applies [2].

Providers established in third countries must appoint an authorised representative established in the Union by written mandate before making their high-risk AI systems available on the Union market [3].

Providers may exceptionally process special categories of personal data to ensure bias detection and correction in relation to high-risk AI systems under certain conditions [2][3][4][5]. This processing must be strictly necessary and subject to appropriate safeguards for the fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons [2][3][4][5]. Furthermore, the bias detection and correction cannot be effectively fulfilled by processing other data, including synthetic or anonymised data [2]. Specific conditions that must be met include ensuring the data is deleted after bias correction or the end of its retention period [3], securing the data with strict controls to prevent misuse [4], and applying technical limitations and privacy-preserving measures like pseudonymisation [5].

The AI Act prohibits the placing on the market, putting into service, or use of an AI system that generates or manipulates realistic images, videos, audio or similar material of an identifiable natural person’s intimate parts, or of an identifiable natural person engaged in sexually explicit activities, without that person’s freely-given, specific, informed, unambiguous and explicit consent for that generation or manipulation [1]. An AI system that manipulates material in a way that does not increase the exposure of any depicted intimate parts or alter the nature of any depicted sexually explicit activities shall not constitute manipulation for the purposes of paragraph 1, first subparagraph, point (ba) [2].

The use of an AI system for making risk assessments of natural persons to assess or predict the risk of a natural person committing a criminal offence, based solely on the profiling of a natural person or on assessing their personality traits and characteristics, is prohibited [1]. However, this prohibition does not apply to AI systems that support the human assessment of a person's involvement in a criminal activity when that assessment is already based on objective and verifiable facts directly linked to the criminal activity [1]. Furthermore, AI systems intended to assess the personality traits and characteristics or past criminal behaviour of natural persons or groups are listed as high-risk in law enforcement contexts [2].

The use of biometric categorisation systems that deduce or infer a natural person's sexual orientation or religious beliefs is prohibited [1]. Furthermore, AI systems intended for biometric categorisation based on sensitive or protected attributes or characteristics through inference are listed as high-risk AI systems [2].

AI systems intended to analyse and filter job applications are considered high-risk AI systems [1]. These systems fall under the area of employment, workers’ management and access to self-employment [1]. High-risk AI systems must be designed and developed so that natural persons can effectively oversee them while they are in use [2].

AI systems intended to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score are listed as high-risk AI systems [1]. However, an exception exists for AI systems used for the purpose of detecting financial fraud [1].

AI systems solely used for non-safety related aspects such as user assistance, performance optimisation, service efficiency, automation, or convenience or quality control shall not qualify as safety components [1a]. However, AI systems whose failure or malfunctioning would endanger health and safety shall qualify as safety components [1b]. For the purposes of this Regulation, a 'safety component' is a component of a product or of an AI system that fulfills a safety function for that product or AI system, or the failure or malfunctioning of which endangers the health and safety of persons or property [5](14).

AI systems intended to be used as safety components in the management and operation of critical digital infrastructure, road traffic, or in the supply of water, gas, heating or electricity are considered high-risk AI systems [1]. Furthermore, AI systems whose failure or malfunctioning would endanger health and safety qualify as safety components [3]. High-risk AI systems must be as resilient as possible regarding errors, faults or inconsistencies [4].

Providers of AI systems that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text content must ensure the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated [1]. Deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated [3]. Furthermore, deployers must disclose that text generated or manipulated by an AI system intended to inform the public on matters of public interest has been artificially generated or manipulated [3].

For AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons, the concerned natural persons must be informed that they are interacting with an AI system, unless it is obvious from the point of view of a natural person who is reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect [1]. The information referred to in paragraphs 1 to 4 must be provided to the natural persons concerned in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure [2]. Deployers must disclose that content constituting a deep fake has been artificially generated or manipulated [3]. For text published with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest, deployers must disclose that the text has been artificially generated or manipulated [3].

Providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, generating synthetic audio, image, video or text content, that have been placed on the market before 2 August 2026 shall take the necessary steps in order to comply with Article 50(2) by 2 December 2026 [2].

A general-purpose AI model is presumed to have high impact capabilities if the cumulative amount of computation used for its training, measured in floating point operations, is greater than $10^{25}$ [1][2]. The Commission may also consider the amount of computation used for training, measured in floating point operations or indicated by other variables like estimated cost, estimated time, or estimated energy consumption [2][3].

Providers of general-purpose AI models are required to draw up and keep up-to-date the technical documentation of the model [1]. This documentation must include information about the model's training and testing process and the results of its evaluation [1]. The technical documentation must contain at least certain information, which is appropriate to the size and risk profile of the model [2][3][4][5].

Providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk must perform model evaluation using standardized protocols and tools, which includes adversarial testing to identify and mitigate systemic risks [1]. They are also required to assess and mitigate possible systemic risks at the Union level, covering their sources from development, placing on the market, or use [1]. Furthermore, these providers must maintain, document, and report relevant information about serious incidents and corrective measures to the AI Office and national competent authorities without undue delay [1]. They must also ensure an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for both the general-purpose AI model and its physical infrastructure [1].

Providers of general-purpose AI models that have been placed on the market before 2 August 2025 shall take the necessary steps in order to comply with the obligations laid down in this Regulation by 2 August 2027 [1].

For an undertaking, non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices referred to in Article 5 is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 35 000 000 or up to 7 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher [1]. For Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies, non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices referred to in Article 5 is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 1 500 000 [2].

The supply of incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to notified bodies or national competent authorities in reply to a request can be subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 7 500 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 1 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher [1]. For providers of general-purpose AI models, the Commission may impose fines not exceeding 3 % of their annual total worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher, if they supplied incorrect, incomplete or misleading information [2]. When the AI Office requests information, it must indicate the potential fines provided for in Article 99(5) for supplying incorrect or misleading information [3]. Furthermore, a request for information must indicate the fines provided for in Article 101 for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information [4].

When deciding on the amount of an administrative fine, all relevant circumstances of the specific situation must be taken into account [1][2][3][4][5]. Specifically, authorities may regard factors such as any other aggravating or mitigating factor, like financial benefits gained or losses avoided from the infringement [1]. They also consider the degree of cooperation with national competent authorities to remedy the infringement and mitigate adverse effects [2]. Furthermore, the size, annual turnover, and market share of the infringing operator are considered [4]. Finally, authorities look at whether administrative fines have previously been applied by other market surveillance authorities for the same infringement [3] or by other authorities for infringements of other Union or national law resulting from the same activity [5].

The Commission may impose fines on providers of general-purpose AI models not exceeding 3 % of their annual total worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher [1]. Fines imposed under this Article must be effective, proportionate, and dissuasive [4]. Before making a decision, the Commission must communicate its preliminary findings to the provider and allow it an opportunity to be heard [3]. The Court of Justice of the European Union has unlimited jurisdiction to review decisions made by the Commission regarding these fines [2].

Downstream providers have the right to lodge a complaint alleging an infringement of this Regulation [2]. A complaint must be duly reasoned and include at least the point of contact of the provider of the general-purpose AI model concerned [2]. It must also describe the relevant facts, the provisions of this Regulation concerned, and the reason why the downstream provider believes the provider infringed the Regulation [2]. Furthermore, the downstream provider may include any other relevant information, including information gathered on its own initiative [2].

Deployers of high-risk AI systems must keep automatically generated logs under their control for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, of at least six months, unless Union or national law dictates otherwise [1]. Providers of high-risk AI systems must keep the logs automatically generated by their high-risk AI systems under their control for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, of at least six months, unless applicable Union or national law provides otherwise [2].
